name: Aurantii Fructus Immaturus (zhishi) flavonoid tablets
short: Bitter orange/synephrine supplements, not these tablets: stroke, heart disease (cases); BP rose in trials. Rats: zhishi cut tacrolimus levels. Tablets (299 vs 99 placebo): related events 6.0% vs 8.1%.
text: This entry covers Aurantii Fructus Immaturus (zhishi), a Chinese herb from the Citrus genus, taken by mouth as flavonoid tablets. The tablet trial abstracts do not name the plant species or say whether the tablets contain synephrine. Other PubMed records describe Aurantii Fructus Immaturus as Citrus aurantium (bitter orange), or as coming from two different species, Citrus aurantium and C. sinensis; one lists it as Zhishi among four Citrus herbs in which synephrine was measured; and a case report describes the unripe fruit of Citrus aurantium as also known as zhi shi. A rat study describes zhishi as the unripe fruit of Citrus aurantium. The tablets: in a phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled trial at 7 centres in China, with 299 people with functional dyspepsia on the tablets and 99 on placebo for 4 weeks, intervention-related adverse events occurred in 6.02% (18 people) with the tablets and 8.08% (8 people) with placebo, all adverse events related to the tablets were mild, and no serious adverse events were recorded. In a double-blind trial against domperidone (120 and 119 patients), 22 adverse events (1 moderate) occurred with the tablets (19.17%) and 43 (3 moderate) with domperidone (36.13%). Bitter orange and synephrine products (not these tablets; how far they apply depends on the tablets' species and synephrine content, which the trial abstracts do not give): a case report describes a 52-year-old woman who had an adverse reaction after a dry extract of unripe Citrus aurantium fruit taken as a weight-loss supplement (the abstract does not describe the reaction; its title calls the extract adrenergic). A 2023 review of 30 case reports (35 patients) after synephrine-containing pre-workout supplements found chest pain, palpitations, fainting and dizziness most often, with ischaemic heart disease, heart rhythm disorders and cerebrovascular disease as common diagnoses; five patients were left disabled or still on medication, and caffeine could not be excluded as a cause. Case reports describe ischaemic stroke in a 38-year-old man after a week of a supplement containing synephrine (which the authors say comes from Citrus aurantium) and caffeine, and ischaemic colitis 1 week after starting a bitter orange weight-loss supplement, resolving after it was stopped. A meta-analysis of placebo-controlled human trials of bitter orange extracts and p-synephrine (18 articles) found that systolic and diastolic blood pressure rose with prolonged use (by 6.37 and 4.33 mmHg). In contrast, in a placebo-controlled crossover trial in 18 healthy adults, one dose of bitter orange extract containing 49 mg of p-synephrine caused no significant changes in heart rate, systolic blood pressure, ECGs or blood tests, and no adverse effects were reported; and a review argues that in the published case reports, all involving multi-ingredient supplements, synephrine was never measured and no direct link was shown. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy or children. Interactions: in rats given the transplant medicine tacrolimus by mouth, a zhishi decoction lowered its peak blood level and total exposure by about 72%, while a decoction of the ripe peel did not affect it; the authors suggest zhishi be contraindicated in transplant patients taking tacrolimus because of the risk of rejection. This is an animal study of a decoction, not of the flavonoid tablets. In 12 healthy volunteers, 28 days of a Citrus aurantium supplement (not these tablets) had no significant effect on four drug-metabolising enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP2E1 and CYP3A4).
